hints: Focus on the $\text{-OH}$ group on phenol in every reaction, the benzene ring stays intact except in one case where substitution occurs on the ring.
Remember phenol is acidic enough to lose $\text{H}^+$ to both $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ and $\text{Na(s)}$, think about what anion is left behind.
For reaction 3, recall that phenol in alkaline solution couples with a diazonium ion at the para position to give a highly coloured $\text{N}=\text{N}$ linked product.

For reaction 4, think of the $\text{-OH}$ group as a nucleophile attacking the $\text{C}=\text{O}$ carbon of an acyl chloride to form an ester linkage, with two $\text{-COCl}$ groups you need two phenols.
walkthrough:
See phenol as a weak acid first**
Picture $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ as a benzene ring with an acidic proton on oxygen. The $\text{O-H}$ bond can break to give $\text{H}^+$ and the phenoxide ion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$. The negative charge is delocalised into the ring, which is why phenol is more acidic than an alcohol. In reactions 1 and 2 you are simply removing that proton, the ring does nothing.

Form sodium phenoxide in reactions 1 and 2**
With $\text{NaOH(aq)}$: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ With $\text{Na(s)}$: $$2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2$$ In both cases the organic product is the same, sodium phenoxide, which you can write as $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ or $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$. Do not draw ring substitution here.

Couple to make an azo dye in reaction 3**
Here you have benzenediazonium ion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+$ plus phenol in $\text{NaOH}$ at $4^{\circ}\text{C}$. Cold alkaline conditions tell you this is azo coupling, electrophilic substitution on the activated phenol ring. The diazonium $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^+$ acts as electrophile and links para to the $\text{-OH}$ (or $\text{-O}^-$) group: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+ + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH} + \text{H}^+$$ That gives $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_5$, an orange azo compound with an extended conjugated system.

Make a diester with terephthaloyl chloride in reaction 4**
The last reagent is benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl dichloride, $\text{ClOC-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COCl}$, which has two highly electrophilic $\text{-COCl}$ groups. Phenol $\text{-OH}$ attacks each $\text{C}=\text{O}$, displacing $\text{Cl}^-$ as $\text{HCl}$ and forming a phenyl ester linkage $\text{-COO-C}_6\text{H}_5$. With excess phenol both ends react: $$2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{ClOC-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COCl} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OOC-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOC}_6\text{H}_5 + 2\text{HCl}$$ So the product is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCOC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CO}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$.

Final answer: Reaction 1: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$ (sodium phenoxide).
Reaction 2: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$ (sodium phenoxide).
Reaction 3: $\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_5$ (para isomer, 4-hydroxyazobenzene) or $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$.
Reaction 4: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCOC}_6\text{H}_4\text{CO}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ (diphenyl benzene-1,4-dioate, phenyl ester).

hints: Compare acidity: ethanol is a weaker acid than phenol so it will not react with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, and it has no activated ring for coupling, but think about which reagents react with any $\text{-OH}$ group.
walkthrough:
Sort by what needs phenol speciality**
Ethanol $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ also has an $\text{-OH}$ group, so it can act as a proton donor to very strong bases and as a nucleophile, just like phenol. It gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa}$ with $\text{Na}$ and an ethyl ester with an acyl chloride. That matches reactions 2 and 4.

Rule out the phenol only reactions**
Ethanol will not neutralise $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ because it is a much weaker acid than phenol, so reaction 1 is phenol only. It also has no benzene ring, so it cannot undergo azo coupling with a diazonium ion like reaction 3. Therefore only 2 and 4 are similar.
